Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a writing prompt for an audio guide at Glass Harbor Museum, for the exhibition Tides in the Foundry. it’s in the museum’s old pump hall, built in 1912, beside the harbor. Visitors usually have about 35 minutes, and I want the guide to connect the working harbor with the nearby estuary without making the whole thing sound like a lecture. Please ask for a complete script, not just an outline. It should be for adults and families, and work when read aloud by one guide voice. Keep the language welcoming and concrete. We don’t need sound-production directions or an invented character talking to the listener.

There are eight numbered stops, and the objects are already chosen below, so please keep the order and use the supplied facts rather than swapping objects or adding a different history. Each stop should be around 70 to 95 spoken words. Add a brief welcome of about 40 to 60 words before the stops, and a short closing after them. The building is active, so visitors might hear ordinary room noise. Don’t promise silence or assume everyone is listening with headphones. The route needs to be clear early in the welcome, because it affects which object someone hears first.

The route has two real possibilities: if the north door is open, visitors should start at stop 1 and follow the numbered route through stop 8. If the north door is closed for conservation work, visitors should instead start at stop 5 at the west landing, continue through stops 6, 7, and 8, then use the printed map to return to stops 1 through 4. Please include both directions, not just a general note that the route might change. Don’t describe stop 5 as though it comes after stop 4 for someone on the alternate route. Since that visitor hears 5 first, keep the wording at the next stops understandable without assuming they’ve already heard the chart or the bench story. The route can still use the printed stop numbers.

The objects and details, for the numbered section of the prompt, are these. 1 is a harbor chart from 1936, with pencil annotations by surveyor Lena Ortiz. It shows the channel before dredging; don’t turn the chart into a claim about who owned the harbor. 2 is a brass tide gauge installed on the breakwater in 1948 and replaced in 1971. We have those dates, but no supplied readings to quote. 3 is a dockworker’s lunch tin, loaned by a dockworker’s family. The initials E.N. are on it; that is not enough to claim it belonged to every worker, or to make up a biography. 4 is a glass-float maker’s bench with four wooden molds. Float production there ended in 1986. These are small things, but I’d like the script to help people notice that tools and records can tell different kinds of stories.

5 is the cast-iron sluice wheel from Reed Point marsh. It was removed in 1999 and turned a gate controlling water flow. 6 is a sound installation built from three channels of interviews about tides and machinery. Visitors may listen, but the script must still make sense if somebody chooses not to. 7 is a storm ledger from 1978 recording water levels at the quay. Its pages are warped. We don’t know from the supplied information that one storm caused all the damage, so don’t say that. 8 is a cabinet of estuary samples collected in 2023 from three sites, with labels for salinity and turbidity. The research is ongoing, and please don’t give it a conclusion or say that the estuary has recovered or is clean. Keep the stops connected to the objects rather than adding facts about the whole city that we haven’t provided.

A couple of existing voices can be quoted, but only where they fit naturally. Curator Mara Bell described the stain on a beam this way: “the water left its handwriting here”. In an oral history, dockworker Eli Navarro said, “we could smell the tide before we saw it”. Keep both quotations as direct quotations and attach them to the right speakers; don’t present either as a label on one of the eight objects. The quotations are optional if they make a stop awkward, but don’t invent more quotations. I’d like the overall tone to be curious and respectful, not sentimental about industrial work and not overly technical. Don’t force a big lesson into each stop.

Please make stop 7 self-contained. In particular, if someone has skipped stop 6 or could not hear it over room noise, they should still understand what the ledger is and what the recorded water levels refer to. Avoid wording such as “as you heard in the sound piece” that makes listening to stop 6 necessary. That matters with the alternate route too, because people can choose how much to listen to and may hear the stops out of the usual order. Keep uncertainty about the 1978 damage and the ongoing sample research intact. The final paragraph of the requested script should give visitors a simple way to finish the visit, without suggesting they have reached a conclusion about harbor or estuary conditions.", "output": "Write a complete, spoken-word audio guide script for the Glass Harbor Museum exhibition *Tides in the Foundry*, located in the museum’s former pump hall, built in 1912 beside the harbor. The audience is adults and families; visitors typically have about 35 minutes. Connect the working harbor with the nearby estuary in a welcoming, concrete way, without making the guide sound like a lecture. Use one guide voice. Do not add an invented character, sound-production directions, or unsupported history.

Include a welcome of about 40–60 words, eight numbered stops in the supplied order, each about 70–95 spoken words, and a short closing. Explain the route in the welcome:
- If the north door is open, visitors start at stop 1 and follow the numbered route through stop 8.
- If the north door is closed for conservation work, visitors start at stop 5 at the west landing, continue through stops 6, 7, and 8, then use the printed map to return to stops 1 through 4.

Include both route instructions. Keep the stop numbers, but write the stops so the alternate route makes sense: do not imply that stop 5 follows stop 4 for visitors starting at stop 5, or assume that they have already heard about the chart or the bench. Visitors may hear ordinary room noise and may choose not to listen to a stop; do not promise silence or assume headphone use.

Use these objects and supplied facts for the numbered stops. Do not replace them with other objects or add unsupported city history:
1. A 1936 harbor chart with pencil annotations by surveyor Lena Ortiz. It shows the channel before dredging. Do not make a claim about who owned the harbor.
2. A brass tide gauge installed on the breakwater in 1948 and replaced in 1971. No readings are supplied to quote.
3. A dockworker’s lunch tin loaned by a dockworker’s family, with the initials E.N. Do not claim the tin belonged to every worker or invent a biography.
4. A glass-float maker’s bench with four wooden molds. Float production there ended in 1986.
5. A cast-iron sluice wheel from Reed Point marsh, removed in 1999, which turned a gate controlling water flow.
6. A sound installation made from three channels of interviews about tides and machinery. Visitors may listen, but the guide must remain understandable if they do not.
7. A storm ledger from 1978 recording water levels at the quay. Its pages are warped. The supplied facts do not establish that one storm caused all the damage.
8. A cabinet of estuary samples collected in 2023 from three sites, labeled for salinity and turbidity. Research is ongoing; do not conclude that the estuary has recovered or is clean.

Help visitors notice that tools and records can tell different kinds of stories, without forcing a lesson into every stop. The tone should be curious and respectful, not sentimental about industrial work or overly technical. Two existing quotations may be used where they fit naturally: curator Mara Bell described the stain on a beam as “the water left its handwriting here”; in an oral history, dockworker Eli Navarro said, “we could smell the tide before we saw it”. Keep each quotation attached to the correct speaker and as direct speech. Do not present either as a label on one of the eight objects or invent additional quotations. The quotations are optional if they do not fit naturally.

Make stop 7 self-contained. Explain what the ledger is and what its recorded water levels refer to even if a visitor skipped stop 6 or could not hear it over room noise. Do not make understanding stop 7 depend on the sound installation or use wording such as “as you heard in the sound piece”. Keep the uncertainty about the ledger’s warped pages and the ongoing sample research intact. End with a simple way for visitors to finish the visit, without suggesting that they have reached a conclusion about harbor or estuary conditions."}]
